Publication of Harold Rosenberg's “The American Action Painters”
Rosenberg, a contributor to the Surrealist magazine VVV during the war, invents the figure of the individual artist excavating himself; he defines the canvas as “an arena in which to act.”
Publication of Harold Rosenberg's essay “Action Painting” in Art News

A founding essay describing the canvas as an arena in which to act rather than a space of representation; at the time one could see every New York exhibition on a lunch break, recognition remaining the preserve of Picasso, Paris, and the dead.
Harold Rosenberg's statement on action painting
In ARTnews, Rosenberg declares that the action painting is of the same metaphysical substance as the artist's existence and that the new painting abolishes every distinction between art and life.
Impressed by the mute poetry of Rauschenberg's white canvases, Cage writes 4'33'', an interval of absolute silence lasting as long as the title indicates (four minutes thirty-three seconds)

Taking part in John Cage's Theater Piece No. 7

A collective theatrical event; descriptions vary. According to Rauschenberg: Cunningham improvises a dance around and through the audience, Cage reads a lecture on Meister Eckhart, M. C. Richards declaims from the top of a ladder, Tudor plays the piano, Rauschenberg projects slides of his paintings while playing old records on a hand-cranked Victrola.
Summer 1952: Theater Piece #1, the first Happening

Over the summer, the friendship with Cage and Cunningham grows stronger. He takes part in an untitled event organized by Cage in the dining hall, later called Theater Piece #1, now considered the first Happening.

During his extended visit of 1952, Cage introduces overlapping activities and narrative fragmentation: teachers and students carry out short timed scripts, unrelated events scattered through the space, impossible to take in all at once. Recognized as the first “happening.”

An event sometimes titled Untitled Event, later proclaimed the first “happening”: segments of fixed duration, tasks assigned to the performers, instruments or tools agreed in advance — a regulated structure allowing maximum unpredictability.
Theater Piece No. 1 (the dining hall event)

Disparate and disputed accounts: to whom did Cage give the script? The surviving fragment was found in the Merce Cunningham archives (where Cernovich and Rauschenberg worked). David Weinrib says Tudor played Water Music; other accounts speak of a piece for prepared piano; Tudor himself vaguely remembers Water Music. Lou Harrison found the whole thing “quite boring.”

Conception of Theater Piece No. 1

In early August 1952, Cage and David Tudor (who came to the college in 1951 as Litz's piano accompanist) devise a performance by multiple participants carrying out separate activities over overlapping time segments totaling forty-five minutes: Olson and Richards read their poetry, the student Rauschenberg shows his paintings and plays records or projects slides, Cunningham dances, Tudor plays the piano, Cage reads a prepared lecture on Zen and the medieval mystic Meister Eckhart.
In early August, Cage and Tudor devise the idea of a performance by multiple participants carrying out separate activities during overlapping time segments totaling forty-five minutes.
Performance of Theater Piece No. 1

Olson and Richards read their poems from a ladder; Rauschenberg shows his paintings, plays records or projects slides (including upside-down slides, probably onto a slanted canopy made of his monochrome White Paintings); Cunningham dances; Tudor plays the piano (probably Water Music, premiered in May 1952 at the New School); films probably projected by Cernovich; Cage reads a prepared lecture on Zen and Meister Eckhart; hot coffee is served in cups placed on each seat, some already used as ashtrays; a dog barks at Cunningham throughout the piece.
Departure for Italy with Cy Twombly

At the end of summer 1952, he leaves BMC for Italy with Twombly (whom he met at the Art Students League), sharing Twombly's Virginia Museum of Arts travel grant. They travel through Italy, France, and Spain before the money runs out.

White paintings made not as an extreme gesture but as an experiment: to see whether there would be anything to look at; the painting takes in the transient images of its surroundings (bluer in late afternoon, white in the morning). No one ever bought one, but for him they remain very full.
John Cage's first happening
Cage stages the first “happening,” a founding event of American theater.

Cage organizes his famous “Happening”: Olson reads poems from the top of a ladder, more scapegoat than high priest; a backdrop of Rauschenberg's white paintings, scratchy Edith Piaf records played at double speed, Cunningham dancing with a stray dog that wandered onto the stage.
MoMA acquires the first photographs

Edward Steichen, director of MoMA's photography department, acquires Untitled (Interior of an Old Carriage) (ca. 1949, taken in Lafayette, Louisiana) and Untitled (Cy on Bench) (1951, made at Black Mountain) — the first works by Rauschenberg to enter a museum, six years before any other acquisition.
Premiere of 4'33" by David Tudor

Tudor sets the handwritten sheets (staves with empty measures) on the piano; at the start of each section he closes the lid, checks a stopwatch, turns the pages, then opens the lid again at the end of each section.
